document.title: Routing From the Submission Viewer
document.headline: Preserve the log, route a copy, and work from buffers.

workCoverage.coverageDescription: Describes the next architectural step after a working submission capture-and-view pipeline: human routing from readable submission cards into task, meeting-note, suggestion, needs-information, or archive buffers while preserving Submission_Log as an append-only source of truth. The lesson covers routing controls, source-versus-derived records, browser-to-Apps-Script boundaries, sample routed-task data, safe implementation order, testing doctrine, and a future progression from human routing to rules and agent assistance.

subject.mainFocus: Teaching a safe routing architecture in which users classify submission cards while Submission_Log remains immutable and new derived records are created in destination buffers.
subject.description: Instructional reference for turning readable submission cards into tasks, meeting notes, suggestions, needs-information, or archive records without altering the permanent submission history.

narrative.promptingSituation: The capture-and-view pipeline was already working: Google Form submissions were normalized into JSON, written to Submission_Log, emailed, and displayed as readable cards. The next problem was deciding what should happen to a submission after a person reviewed it.
narrative.initialUnderstanding: Routing should not move or rewrite the original submission. The permanent log and the working records answer different questions and therefore need separate storage and behavior.
narrative.intendedOutcome: Define a safe, understandable path from a submission card to a task, meeting note, suggestion, needs-information record, or archive decision, with traceability back to the source.
narrative.approach: Establish the append-only rule, define destination buffers, describe the browser-to-Apps-Script message, distinguish source and routed records, show an example derived task, assign clear tool responsibilities, specify a cautious build sequence, and define failure-based tests.

problemsEncountered.problem: A submission needs to become actionable without destroying or confusing the original history.
problemsEncountered.effect: Moving or editing source records would make it difficult to reconstruct what was originally submitted.
problemsEncountered.resolution: Keep Submission_Log append-only and create linked derived records in destination buffers.

unsuccessfulApproaches.approach: Move records out of Submission_Log when routing.
unsuccessfulApproaches.whyItWasTried: Moving a row might appear to simplify categorization.
unsuccessfulApproaches.whyItDidNotWork: It would destroy the permanent record of what was submitted and mix evidence management with operational work.
unsuccessfulApproaches.whatWasLearned: Classification should create a derivative rather than relocate the source.

unsuccessfulApproaches.approach: Send the entire JSON object from the browser during routing.
unsuccessfulApproaches.whyItWasTried: The browser already displays the record and could appear to have all required data.
unsuccessfulApproaches.whyItDidNotWork: The browser copy should not replace the authoritative record stored in Submission_Log.
unsuccessfulApproaches.whatWasLearned: The browser should send only identity and intent; the controller should resolve the source record.

turningPoints.title: The log and buffers were assigned different questions

turningPoints.effectOnDirection: Traceability and auditability became structural properties of the workflow.

narrative.methodEstablished: Capture first, preserve the log, route a copy, link every derivative to the source submission, and perform operational work from buffers.
narrative.result: The document defines a complete routing architecture, safe implementation sequence, and failure-based test doctrine for extending the Submission Viewer into an operational workflow.
lessonsLearned: Historical evidence and operational records should not share mutation rules.
A route is a decision that creates a new record, not a movement of the source.
The browser should communicate identity and intent while the server resolves authoritative data.
A valid routing system must prove that the source record remains unchanged.
Human routing can create the structured examples needed for later rule-based or agent-assisted routing.
narrative.directionChange: The system moves from passive capture and display toward controlled operational routing while preserving the original evidence layer.
narrative.narrativeSummary: This lesson converts the existing submission viewer into a blueprint for human-in-the-loop routing: immutable source history, linked working buffers, server-authoritative source lookup, cautious implementation, explicit tests, and a future path toward automation.

callouts.title: The original log stays intact
callouts.text: Routing creates a linked copy or derivative; it does not move or rewrite the original submission.

callouts.title: The server remains authoritative
callouts.text: The browser sends a submission ID and destination, and Apps Script retrieves the source JSON from the log.

callouts.title: A source change is a failure
callouts.text: The route is valid only if the new buffer record appears and the original log row remains unchanged.

general.summary: A lesson on safely routing immutable submission records into mutable working buffers.

technical.summary: Cards.html should send only submission_id and route. Apps Script should resolve the authoritative normalized JSON in Submission_Log and append a linked derived record to the selected Google Sheet buffer.
keyPoints: Task_Buffer is the first implementation target

projectSpecificLessons: The Submission Viewer is a suitable human-routing surface because it already presents normalized submissions as readable cards.
Task_Buffer should become the source for a future Tasks page rather than reusing Submission_Log as a queue.
generalLessons: Immutable source records and mutable operational records should be separate objects.
Derived records should preserve explicit lineage to their source.
Browser clients should send minimal commands while servers resolve authoritative data.
A failure condition can be more useful than a success description: changing the source log means the routing design is wrong.
Human decisions can establish the labeled examples needed for later automation.

email.subject: Submission Viewer Routing Design
email.body: The next step for the submission viewer is to add human routing from each readable card into separate working buffers. The original Submission_Log will remain unchanged, and every routed task, note, suggestion, information request, or archive record will point back to the source submission. Task_Buffer is the proposed first implementation target.
